snapshot.title: feat: gc mail send --body-file — a mail body has no path that bypasses the shell
snapshot.body:
## Summary

`gc mail send` accepts a body only as a command-line argument (`-m/--message`). There is no way
to pass a body that does not transit a shell string. For the messages that matter most — incident
reports, bug filings, post-mortems — that body must quote shell commands, and quoting them in a
double-quoted argument lets the caller's shell expand them before `gc` is ever invoked.

Request: add `--body-file <path>` to `gc mail send`, mirroring `gh issue create --body-file`.

## Why this is worth a flag rather than documentation

The hazard is selected for by the task. A message *about* a dangerous command is the message most
likely to contain one. The more faithfully an agent documents what went wrong, the more likely its
report is to reproduce it.

It also lands on the worst available target. A rig worker's cwd is the shared rig root, which in a
worktree-per-bead setup routinely holds another agent's staged `--no-commit` merge through a
20-30 minute verification. So the blast radius is other agents' in-flight work, not the sender's.

## What happened here, measured 2026-09-16

An agent composed an incident report whose body quoted git commands in backticks, inside a
double-quoted string passed to `gc mail send -m "..."`. The shell substituted them. Three writes
executed against the shared rig root:

```
git reset --soft main       -> cleared MERGE_HEAD, destroying another agent's staged merge
git reset --hard <sha>      -> moved the main branch ref backward
git reset --soft <base>
```

Six merge commits became unreachable from `main` for about three minutes, and a `bead-land.sh`
process died under `set -e` when the merge it was verifying was deleted beneath it. That land had
been running ~39 minutes. Everything was recovered; nothing was lost.

## Scope, stated precisely

This is **not** a code-execution defect in `gc`. The expansion happens in the caller's shell before
`gc` receives anything, and no attacker-controlled input reaches `gc`. I checked `SECURITY.md` and
am deliberately filing this in public for that reason.

What `gc` can do is offer a path that does not require a shell string in the first place.

## Suggested shape

```
gc mail send <to> -s "subject" --body-file ./report.md
gc mail send <to> -s "subject" --body-file -      # stdin
```

Mirror on `gc mail reply` if it shares the code path.

Acceptance: a file whose contents include a backticked `git reset --hard HEAD~5`, a `$(...)`, and a
`${...}` transmits byte-identically and executes nothing.

## Current workaround

A quoted heredoc plus command substitution, which is inert:

```bash
cat > /tmp/body.txt <<'EOF'
backticks are inert in here
EOF
gc mail send <to> -s "subject" -m "$(cat /tmp/body.txt)"
```

It works. It is also easy to forget under incident pressure, which is when it is needed.

Version: gascity 1.4.1 (Homebrew bottle, macOS).

snapshot.title: feat(controller): poke the reconciler on provider session events instead of waiting for the next patrol scan
snapshot.body:
## What this changes

A session that dies is noticed when the controller's patrol next scans for it. A provider
that pushes session events already knows seconds earlier, and nothing consumed that. This
adds one consumer: `cmd/gc/session_event_pump.go` bridges the provider's event stream into
the session reconciler's existing poke channel.

herdr implements `runtime.SessionEventProvider`, so it gets this. tmux has no stream and
is untouched. Patrol cadence is unchanged, the reconciler's behavior is unchanged, and
there is no new configuration. The reconcile simply runs sooner, on a signal that was
already arriving and being dropped.

## How it behaves

The pump is level-triggered throughout: an event is a hint to go look, never a fact to act
on.

- Attributed `exited` and `closed` events poke immediately.
- Resync events poke on a trailing delay (15s, re-armed per resync). Every connection
  cycle leads with a resync, including the benign resubscribe the stream runs for each
  newly detected agent pane, and an immediate poke would land a reconcile inside the very
  start wave that triggered it.
- One minute after the first resync of a burst, the poke lands regardless. The last re-arm
  is clamped to what remains of that window, so the cap is the poke's deadline rather than
  the point after which one more whole delay may still run.
- Unattributed pane events are dropped. Such a poke races an in-flight create's metadata
  stamp and rolls the pending create back.

The pump deliberately publishes no "the stream is healthy" signal. herdr's
`SubscribeSessionEvents` returns a channel and a nil error unconditionally and connects
behind it, retrying forever with capped backoff, so a subscription to an unreachable
provider is indistinguishable from a live one. `streaming()` documents that, and says
outright that it must not be used to decide to poll less: a stream that exists is not a
stream that has delivered.

## What is deliberately not here

**Delivering queued nudges on idle events.** That consumer was written, reviewed, and then
removed from this change. Routing every delivery through one shared worker turns a
per-session hang into a city-wide one: `runtime.Provider.Nudge` takes no context at all,
herdr's implementation uses `context.Background()`, and the client applies no timeout, so a
hung prompt would block delivery for every other session and ignore cancellation. The
per-session pollers that exist today confine that blast radius. Retiring them is only safe
once each delivery is bounded and the worker can abandon a hung one, which is a change of
its own.

**A `[daemon].session_patrol_interval` that stretched the patrol while events were
flowing.** Also written, also removed. The run loop cancels pending event-driven fires on
every patrol tick, and says why in a comment: a patrol scans every reconciler state
authoritatively. A patrol that skips the session phases makes that false, so a death poke
armed a second before a patrol was cancelled by a patrol that then did not scan, and
detection waited for the stretched interval. It was an optimisation layered on a feature
that is worth having without it.

## One unrelated test

`TestNewCityRuntimeWiresAssignedWorkDeferTracker`. The assigned-work defer tracker is
constructed in `newCityRuntime` and consumed through an option, and every test for it
drives the option directly, so dropping the construction leaves the suite green while the
backstop is dead in production. That happened during this work, and only the unused-symbol
linter caught it, because the builder lost its last caller at the same moment; losing just
the call would have been silent.

The test asserts both halves, and it pins the production call site through `go/parser`
rather than a text search. A text search cannot tell code from a comment, so commenting
the argument out would leave the backstop dead with the test still green.

## Test plan

- `gofmt`, `go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`: clean.
- `go test ./internal/config/ ./internal/session/ ./internal/runtime/herdr/... ./internal/testpolicy/... ./test/docsync/`: pass.
- `go test ./cmd/gc/`: pass (279s).
- `make check-docs`: pass.
- `golangci-lint run ./cmd/gc/... ./internal/config/... ./internal/session/... ./internal/runtime/herdr/...`: clean.
- Live journey against herdr 0.8.0 (`make test-herdr-live`, which now covers the `cmd/gc`
  journey as well): an agent's natural process exit lands a reconcile poke with no polling.
  The opt-in predicate and the single subprocess the live tier shells out to moved into
  `internal/runtime/herdr/herdrtest` so the provider tier and `cmd/gc` share one gate and
  one bounded polling helper. Each `report-agent` invocation is bounded at 2s, because an
  unbounded call inside the helper's poll condition would mean its 10s bound was never
  reachable and a hung server would surface as the outer test timeout instead.
- No test sleeps. The pump's timer behavior runs inside `testing/synctest` bubbles, where
  the trailing-delay and cap assertions are exact rather than approximate.
- Mutation checks on the wiring guard: deleting the tracker argument fails the test,
  commenting it out fails it, and the real code passes.

snapshot.title: cmd-gc-productmetrics-testhook runs at 92-95% of its 5-minute budget on main; its six tests take 0.87s and the rest is compile
snapshot.body:
## Symptom

`cmd-gc-productmetrics-testhook` runs at 92–95% of its `timeout-minutes: 5` budget on `main`, so it fails as a cancellation ("The operation was canceled") on whichever PR happens to add a few seconds. It is a required-path job, so that reads as a red gate with no failing test in the log.

Measured across runs on 2026-09-16 (UTC):

| branch | duration |
|---|---|
| `main` @ `9700d9a48` | 4m37 |
| a branch with no `go.mod` change | 4m44 |
| a branch that changed `go.sum` | **5m05 → killed** |

## Root cause

The budget is buying compile time, not test time, on a runner the budget was not sized for.

From the job's own timing artifact (`timing-cmd-gc-productmetrics-testhook-attempt-1`, run 35040648087, `main` @ `9700d9a48`):

- `cmd/gc` package unit: **0.869 s**
- every test in it: sub-second; six tests, **0.87 s total**

against a 4m37 job. The remainder is `go build` of `cmd/gc` under `-tags productmetrics_testhook`.

The job requests `runs-on: ${{ needs.runner-policy.outputs.runner_32vcpu }}` (`.github/workflows/ci.yml:626`), but `runner-policy` resolves that to `ubuntu-latest` for every login outside the maintainer list — the same artifact's runner block reports `"cpu_count": 4`. So most runs compile `cmd/gc` on four cores inside a five-minute wall.

The `go.sum` sensitivity follows: `actions/setup-go`'s cache key includes `go.sum`, so any dependency change makes that build cold, and cold is what goes over.

## Reproduction

Open a PR that changes `go.sum` at all, on a fork or from a non-maintainer login, and watch `cmd/gc product metrics testhook`. Or read the timing artifact of any recent `main` run and compare the summed test durations against the job duration.

## Environment

`main` @ `9700d9a48`, `ubuntu-latest` (4 vCPU), `actions/setup-go@4a36011`, Go per `go.mod`.

## Proposed fixes, either

1. **Give the job a warm build cache.** It is the only `cmd/gc`-building job with no warm step before it; the surrounding jobs go through `setup-gascity-ubuntu`. That attacks the 4m23 rather than the wall.
2. **Size the budget for the runner the job actually gets** — 10–12 minutes gives real margin at 4 vCPU.

(1) is the better fix; (2) is the one-line stopgap. A gate at 95% of budget reports on runner speed rather than on the code.

snapshot.title: bug: pool seats retired mid-claim because alias-form claims are invisible to the keep-awake and drain-ack close gates
snapshot.body:
### Gas City version
main `ed146d8d9` (2026-09-02); the unit-level reproduction also holds on `af596339d` (2026-09-14).

### Environment
Linux (Fedora 44), tmux runtime, opencode-backed pool agents (gastown pack `gastown.polecat`, `max_active_sessions = 10`).

### Reproduction
1. Route several beads to a pool template; seats claim them with `gc hook --claim`. The claim's `assignee` is the seat alias (`GC_ALIAS`, e.g. `rig/gastown.nux`), while the session bead's `session_name` is the tmux form (`rig--gastown__nux`).
2. Let template demand drop (other beads finish) while one seat still holds an `in_progress` claim.
3. Watch the reconciler: that seat is closed with `session drained: pool slot retired by reconciler`, followed immediately by `bead.dead_assignee_reopened` for its claim, and a fresh seat re-primes from zero.

### Expected behavior
A seat holding an `in_progress` claim stays desired (`assigned-work`), is counted by `countAssignedScaleSlots`, and the drain-ack close gate sees its claim.

### Actual behavior
`sessionAssignmentIdentifierRaw`/`RawInfo` and `ComputeAwakeSet`'s `sessionAssigneeMatches` only compare `{bead id, session_name, configured named identity}`. Claims are written under the alias (`session.AssigneeIdentifier` is alias-first), so every pool seat reads as work-free and becomes a scale-down victim. The orphan-release path (`session.AssigneeIdentities`) already honours the alias, which is why the reopen follows the drain within seconds.

### Logs, screenshots, or traces
One city, 24 h, tributary pool: 122 polecat stops, 89 `bead.dead_assignee_reopened`, mean seat life ~20 min, 15–25 % of seats under 3 min; identical under three model providers, so not model-related. With the alias honoured in those three sites (see the linked PR): 22 stops and 0 reopens over the next 24 h.

### Additional context
`TestAssignmentGuardsIgnoreTransientPoolSlotAliases` states slot-form aliases (`<pool>-<n>`) must never keep a session alive. The PR keeps that guard and honours namepool aliases only. If the preferred fix is to claim under a stable identity instead (bead id / session_name), I'm happy to rework it that way.

snapshot.title: fix(mail): supersede recurring digests and retire resolved BLOCKED reports
snapshot.body:
## Problem

The mayor inbox accumulates and never drains, so it stops carrying signal. On
2026-09-15 it grew from 27 to 32 unread messages in one afternoon: 15 BLOCKED
worker reports, 6 hourly Slack alert review digests, and 11 one-off
completions. Two distinct causes, fixed as two separable commits.

1. A recurring order reports **full current state** every hour, so six copies
   of the same state are noise and only the newest matters.
2. A BLOCKED report whose blocker is already cleared stays unread forever.
   `sc-wisp-chkxapn` asked for PR 25 to be merged, which happened;
   `sc-wisp-3d8v85a` asked for the launchd agent to be enabled, which
   happened. Both reports are still sitting there.

## What changes

### `gc mail send --supersede <order>`

A recurring digest names its order. The new message archives the sender's
earlier **unread** messages carrying the same key to the **same** recipient.
Archiving closes the message bead and retains its body, so a superseded digest
stays readable through `gc mail peek` and `bd show` — no history is deleted.

The match is scoped by key, sender, and recipient together, and skips messages
already read. A worker's one-off report carries no key, so no later digest can
retire it.

### `gc mail send --blocked-on <bead>`

An escalation names the bead it waits on. The reader's next `gc mail inbox`
archives the report once that bead closes.

**Mechanism chosen: an explicit annotation plus a sweep on the inbox read
path.** Alternatives rejected:

- **Scrape bead ids out of the subject and body.** Rejected. A message that
  mentions a closed bead in passing would be archived, and the failure mode is
  exactly the one that must never happen: a live escalation disappears. The bead
  description notes that five notices today already named session beads rather
  than messages, which is what text scraping produces.
- **Hook `gc bd close` to archive the mail.** Rejected. It couples the close
  path to the mail package for no gain, and it misses every close that goes
  through `bd` directly rather than `gc bd` — which on this machine is most of
  them.
- **Auto-archive on a timer.** Explicitly forbidden by the bead, and rightly:
  age is not evidence that a blocker is resolved.

The sweep acts only on positive evidence. A bead still open or in progress, a
bead the store cannot read, and a named session or message bead all keep the
report visible. A session bead closes when its session ends, which says nothing
about the blocker. The sweep is advisory: a failure warns on stderr and never
stops the listing, because a stale report beats no listing at all.

A backend that cannot carry metadata rejects both flags rather than dropping
them. A digest whose supersede key vanished would pile up again with no sign
that anything failed.

### Incidental

`cmdMailSend` is gone. It existed only to pass `jsonOut=false` from a branch in
`RunE`, which now passes the flag straight through, leaving the wrapper with no
production caller (`unparam` flagged it).

## Tests

Each acceptance criterion has a test that fails when its guard is removed.

| Test | Proves |
|---|---|
| `TestSupersedeKeyLeavesOnlyTheNewestDigestUnread` | A second digest from the same order to the same recipient leaves exactly **one** unread message, the retained unread body is the **newest**, and the older one is closed with its body intact. |
| `TestSupersedeNeverRetiresUnrelatedMessages` | A one-off worker report, a different order, a different sender, and a different recipient all survive. Six sends, four survivors. |
| `TestArchiveResolvedBlockersOnlyRetiresClosedBlockers` | A message naming a still-open bead, an unknown bead, a closed **session** bead, or no bead at all is never archived. Only the closed work bead's report goes. |
| `TestArchiveResolvedBlockersSkipsReadAndRepeats` | A read message is left alone, and a repeat sweep is a no-op. |
| `TestSendAnnotatedMail*` (3) | The flags reach the message as the keys the backend reads back; a backend without metadata support rejects rather than drops; unannotated mail keeps the plain `Send` path. |
| `TestSweepResolvedBlockersPassesEveryRecipientRoute` | Every resolved recipient route is swept; a provider without the extension is skipped silently; a sweep failure warns but does not fail the listing. |

Mutation check on the guard the criteria hinge on: replacing the key-and-sender
comparison in `supersedePrior` with `if false` makes
`TestSupersedeNeverRetiresUnrelatedMessages` fail with
`unread subjects = [review: second], want 4 messages`.

```
go test ./internal/mail/... ./cmd/gc/ -run 'Mail|Nudge|Supersede|ResolvedBlockers|SendAnnotatedMail|SessionModelPhase0' -count=1   # ok
go test ./internal/api/... ./internal/bootstrap/... -count=1                                                                        # ok
golangci-lint run internal/mail/... cmd/gc/...   # clean, except a pre-existing revive hit in dolt_data_dir_lock_other.go
```

## Overlap with open PRs

Checked 6358, 6371, and 6372 as the bead asked.

- **6358** (`Reject non-message mail mutations`) touches `beadmail.go`, but only
  adds type guards inside `Read`, `MarkRead`, and `MarkUnread`. This PR touches
  `Send` and adds new functions. No conflict, and the two are complementary.
- **6371** is supervisor/launchd only.
- **6372** touches `cmd_nudge.go` and the pending-mail notice, not the send or
  inbox paths changed here.

## Follow-up, not in this PR

`scripts/slack-alert-review.py` in the Stryker-City workspace needs
`--supersede slack-alert-review` added to its `gc mail send` call for the fix to
take effect on the six digests that motivated it. That file sits outside this
repository and another session holds a live claim on it.

Closes sc-rur0b.

snapshot.title: bug: a requested named-session restart can leave a live, promptless runtime — start errors in start_call, never reaches post_start_observe, and nothing retries
snapshot.body:
### Before you continue

- [x] I searched existing issues and did not find a duplicate.
- [x] I read the relevant docs and contributor guidance.

Searched: `resuming session: session already exists`, `post_start_observe`,
`restart-requested no such session`, `session reconciler race prompt`,
`session launched without prompt`, `unprimed session`,
`start_call provider_error session already exists`.

The two nearest hits are **not** this, and I want to be explicit about why,
because both look close:

- **#5593** (closed) matches on the error string `resuming session: session
  already exists`, but it is about `one_shot` **pool** sessions blocking their
  own runtime name after a normal exit. This is a **named** session being
  restarted on request.
- **#4382** (open) is also "born unprimed", but by a different mechanism:
  reconciler-spawned **formula step** sessions whose routing is stamped at
  `bead.created` so `nudge-on-route` never fires. Here the session is a named
  one, the restart was explicitly requested, and the start itself errors.

### Gas City version

`HEAD-e736d74d0` — source build of `e736d74d0` (2026-08-24), with a
source-built `bd` `1.1.0 (dev: main@bf97b73749ac)`.

### Environment

Linux, systemd `--user` supervisor, Dolt-backed stores, `claude` provider,
2 rigs (both suspended — a near-idle city). Named session `mayor`,
`lifecycle` restart-on-request via `gc handoff`.

### Reproduction

1. Have a named, controller-restartable session (here: `mayor`).
2. From inside it, request a restart — `gc handoff`, which sends mail to self
   and then `gc runtime request-restart`.
3. Observe the reconciler's stop/start pair in `supervisor.log`.

It does not reproduce on demand: this is a **race**, and it has now happened
twice in twelve days against ~119 healthy starts in the same log. I am filing
it because both occurrences leave the *same* distinctive signature, so the
signature is probably more useful to you than a recipe.

### Expected behavior

The restarted session receives its rendered template prompt as the first user
message, as it does on every healthy start.

### Actual behavior

The runtime starts and the prompt is never delivered. A `claude` process is
alive in the tmux session, attached and idle, with **zero user records in its
transcript**, and it stays that way indefinitely — 7m08s on this occurrence,
until a human ran `gc session reset mayor`. 15 minutes on the previous one.

Nothing retries: the session is up, so the reconciler is satisfied.

### Logs, screenshots, or traces

The failing restart, `~/.gc/supervisor.log`:

```
session reconciler: clearing restart-requested marker for mayor (bead bl-0odu):
    tmux -u: no such session: mayor
Stopped restart-requested session 'mayor'
session reconciler: provider-health registry unavailable for "claude-mayor";
    treating as green
session lifecycle: op=start wave=0 session=mayor template=mayor
    outcome=start_enqueued duration=0s
session reconciler: starting mayor: resuming session: session already exists:
    session "mayor"
session lifecycle: op=start wave=0 session=mayor template=mayor
    outcome=provider_error duration=351ms phases=[start_call=351ms]
    err=resuming session: session already exists: session "mayor"
Stopped restart-requested session 'mayor'
```

The successful manual reset seven minutes later, same session, same log:

```
session lifecycle: op=start wave=0 session=mayor template=mayor
    outcome=start_enqueued duration=0s
Woke session 'mayor'
session lifecycle: op=start wave=0 session=mayor template=mayor
    outcome=success duration=19.799s
    phases=[start_call=17.727s post_start_observe=2.072s]
```

**The discriminator is `post_start_observe`.** Every healthy start in this log
carries it (~5s + ~2.1s); the failed start has only `start_call` and no `Woke
session` line. The prompt appears to be delivered in that phase, so a start
that errors in `start_call` leaves a live, promptless runtime behind.

The 2026-09-04 occurrence has the same shape with a different error string —
`outcome=success duration=28ms phases=[start_call=28ms]`, no
`post_start_observe` — against ~5s + ~2.1s on the other 118 starts in that
window.

The event log tells the same story more compactly. A requested restart emits
`session.draining` then `session.woke`; across nine prior restarts of this
session the pair is always 32–68s apart, and on the failure the second event
never arrives:

```
14:55:08 -> 14:55:40  +32s      21:00:26 -> 21:01:02  +36s
15:14:44 -> 15:15:52  +68s      21:37:15 -> 21:37:49  +34s
16:39:43 -> 16:40:38  +55s      00:13:45 -> 00:14:44  +59s
18:38:57 -> 18:39:54  +57s      10:09:49 -> (none)
19:11:15 -> 19:11:52  +37s
```

### Additional context

**The apparent mechanism**, offered as a reading of the log rather than as a
claim about the code, which I have not read: the reconciler goes to clear the
restart marker and tmux reports the session already gone. Its bookkeeping then
treats the session as present on the following start — the start takes a
*resume* path — and the resume errors because by then a tmux session named
`mayor` exists again.

**Two things that might matter for the fix:**

1. `provider_error` here is not retried. Whatever the right recovery is, the
   current outcome is a permanently idle session that looks healthy to
   everything watching it.
2. `gc session reset` is a reliable recovery, and we have automated it locally
   behind a zero-user-records predicate. That is a workaround, not a fix, and
   it only works because a session with no user records has no state to lose.

**A detail that may help anyone else hitting this:** a queued nudge cannot
rescue such a session. Ours were dead-lettered with `queued nudge session
fence mismatch` about 29s in — the fence is the continuation epoch rather than
the session id, so a nudge queued across the restart boundary dies with the
old epoch. So the failure is not observable-and-recoverable through the nudge
path; the session has to be replaced.

snapshot.title: docs(herdr): pin a herdr version, and say what the controller does not do yet
snapshot.body:
## What this changes

`docs/reference/herdr-provider.md` told readers the provider is "verified against
herdr 0.7.1+". The plus sign is the problem: 0.7.1 is the oldest release with a
recorded end-to-end validation, not a floor above which the surface is known to
hold. Nothing on the page said the surface had moved, and it has moved twice.

The page now makes the pinning argument from what actually happened:

- 0.7.4 and 0.7.5 altered commands the original adapter depended on.
- 0.8.0 renamed the code herdr returns for a pane with no named agent. That is
  the code the adapter reads to decide whether to paste a nudge instead of
  submitting it through the agent. Under the new spelling it stopped recognising
  that case, so the original failure went back to the caller and the paste never
  happened. Delivery reported an error rather than going quiet, but nothing in the
  build or the default suite went red, because the tests that drive a real binary
  are opt-in. The regression had to be noticed in the field.

So: pin a version in any shared environment, read herdr's own release list rather
than a version named in our docs, and after an upgrade run `make test-herdr-live`
and put a session through a full work cycle.

The page no longer names a current herdr release. A reference page cannot keep
that true, and an out-of-date "current version" reads as authoritative.

## The one known coverage gap

0.8.0 made herdr's agent registry detection-based, so the live journey that drives
the session-event stream waives itself when the installed herdr reports 0.8 or
later rather than asserting against a registry it no longer matches
([#5808](https://github.com/gastownhall/gascity/issues/5808)). That waiver reads
the version, not the registry: a herdr whose version cannot be read or parsed runs
the journey, and on 0.8 its registry assertions then fail. The other real-herdr
journeys (provider lifecycle, pane binding, activity, and the runtime conformance
suite) do run on 0.8; the kind-launch journey needs an installed `claude` binary as
well and skips without one. 0.7.1 remains the version the recorded end-to-end
validation ran against.

That distinction matters to a reader deciding whether to pilot this. "Not covered
on 0.8" would tell them to stay on 0.7; one waived journey out of seven tells them
what to watch instead.

## What is not wired yet

A new section, with one entry: the controller does not consume herdr's
session-event stream. herdr pushes session events and the provider implements
`runtime.SessionEventProvider`, but the only consumer today is the provider's own
activity reporting. The reconciler discovers session state on its periodic pass,
so a session that goes away is noticed on the next pass rather than when the event
arrives.

That costs latency rather than correctness, because each pass reads live state
rather than trusting an event. The delay is bounded by the reconcile interval only
while the controller keeps up; ticks run one at a time, so a busy controller
stretches it.

## Claims that came out of earlier drafts

Four statements were removed or corrected because they did not survive checking
against the code. Recording them here so they do not come back:

- That no error appeared when the 0.8.0 fallback broke. `deliverNudge` returns the
  original error; what was missing was anything making it fail a build.
- That the warm-reuse claim nudge bypasses session-store routing. It does not. The
  reconciler unwraps its typed session store (`session_reconciler.go`,
  `store := sessStore.Store`) and threads that down to the nudge, so both the read
  and the marker write already reach a relocated sessions backend.
- That the controller's added latency is the patrol interval. Ticks are serial, so
  the interval bounds it only while the controller keeps up.
- That the live journeys are waived on 0.8 and later. One of seven is, and that
  waiver is keyed to the version string rather than to the registry it is about.

Startup-prompt redelivery across a continuation-epoch bump was also dropped from
this page: it is a test-coverage gap rather than a behavior gap, and belongs with
the tests. Store-maintenance notifications repeating per interval is real and has
nothing to do with herdr.

## Test plan

Docs-only, one file, no Go changes.

```
go build ./... && go vet ./...
go test ./test/docsync/ ./internal/testpolicy/...
make check-docs
```

All green at this head. Every version-behavior claim on the page is cited to the
adapter code or to the test that covers it; the live-journey counts were derived
by listing the callers of the live gate and of the detection-based-registry skip.

snapshot.title: test(graph): wait on the teardown tail, not the workflow root (ga-pva49c)
snapshot.body:
## What

`TestGraphWorkflowSuccessPath` used `waitForBeadClosed(workflowID)` as the barrier for three assertions about the worktree cleanup's effects: the convoy's `work_dir` being unset (`:77`), the worktree directory being removed (`:85`), and `.cleanup-worktree` appearing in the step report (`:99`). A closed workflow root does not imply any of those have happened, so the test raced the controller and went flaky under full-suite load.

Both graph workflow tests now wait on the teardown's own close via a new `waitForWorkflowTeardown` helper before asserting its effects.

## Why the root is not a barrier

Teardown-scoped work is post-settlement **by contract**, established in #5271 (bead ga-99u0u) and enforced in two places:

- `graphSinkStepIDs` (`internal/formula/graph.go`) omits `gc.scope_role=teardown` steps from `workflow-finalize`'s sinks. Sinking them deadlocks settlement — a teardown's pass condition can wait on the root outcome only finalize produces.
- `processWorkflowFinalize` (`internal/dispatch/runtime.go`) closes the root, then exempts the teardown tail from its terminal subtree sweep (`molecule.TeardownTailExclusion`) so cleanup stays executable afterwards instead of being skip-closed, which would leak the worktree.

Compiling `mol-scoped-work` shows the consequence directly:

```
workflow-finalize          <-blocks- body
workflow-finalize          <-blocks- submit-scope-check
cleanup-worktree.attempt.1 <-blocks- body
cleanup-worktree           <-blocks- body
```

`cleanup-worktree` and `workflow-finalize` are concurrent successors of the body scope with **no edge between them**. Whichever the controller reaches first wins.

The compile test's `assertBefore("…cleanup-worktree", "…workflow-finalize")` compares slice indices in the emitted recipe, not dependency edges, so it never pinned an ordering — which is why this looked guarded and was not.

The integration test was last touched 2026-06-17; the contract changed 2026-08-14 (`517b605302`) and the test was never updated. Both observed failures postdate it: ga-lwnqu9 (2026-09-04, the report assertion) and ga-qhr85l (2026-09-15, `work_dir`).

## Why the retry control is the barrier

`waitForWorkflowTeardown` waits on the cleanup step's **retry control**, not its attempt. The control closes only once the teardown has converged, so it stays correct when `attempt.1` fails transiently and `attempt.2` does the real work. The `.cleanup-worktree` ref suffix matches only that control — `.cleanup-worktree.attempt.1` and `.cleanup-worktree.spec` do not end in it. The worker writes the report line, clears `work_dir` and removes the directory *before* closing the attempt, so a closed control means all three effects are durable.

## Regression guard

`TestGraphWorkflowRootClosesWithoutTeardown` (in-memory, ~10ms, no subprocess or sleep, so no resource-census growth) pins the contract at the dispatch layer: with the teardown withheld from the worker, the root still closes `pass`, the teardown tail is still open, and the convoy still carries `work_dir`.

Verified non-vacuous — removing the teardown-sink exclusion from `graphSinkStepIDs` fails it with the root stuck `in_progress`, which is exactly the #5271 deadlock.

**No production change**: the settlement contract is deliberate and this PR does not touch it.

## Validation

| Gate | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `TestGraphWorkflowSuccessPath` (tags=integration) | PASS (167.70s) |
| `TestGraphWorkflowFailureRunsCleanup` (tags=integration) | PASS (78.73s) |
| `TestGraphWorkflowRootClosesWithoutTeardown` | PASS (~10ms) |
| `make test` | PASS |
| `go vet ./...` (and `-tags integration`) | clean |
| `./internal/testpolicy/...` (resource census) | PASS |

Closes ga-pva49c. Evidence for gate tracker ga-xjh1p4.

`claimFirstEligibleHookCandidate` reclaims only when `hookClaimOptions.AutoReclaimStaleClaims` is true (`cmd/gc/cmd_hook_claim.go:794`). Those options are built in one production place, `cmd/gc/cmd_hook.go:474-482`. git grep -n AutoReclaimStaleClaims -- 'cmd/gc/*.go' ':!*_test.go'

snapshot.title: bug(controller): order-tracking retention runs before the city reports ready
snapshot.body:
### Symptom

After a supervisor restart, the synchronous order-tracking retention pass can delay city readiness. This happens when the store is slow or holds a large closed order-tracking set. Until readiness is published, city-scoped API requests return 404 ("city not found or not running").

We saw about six minutes of this on a city with ~73k closed tracking beads on a slow Dolt server:

```
gc start: ≥1001 closed order-tracking beads detected — retention watchdog will prune automatically (7d TTL default; ...)
startup watchdog: city "westeros" not ready after 2m30s (half of [daemon].start_ready_timeout=5m0s); goroutine dump follows
```

In the goroutine dump, the tick goroutine was inside the sweep:

```
CityRuntime.run -> safeTick -> dispatchOrders -> runOrderTrackingRetentionWatchdog
  -> sweepClosedOrderTrackingRetentionAcrossStoresBounded -> ... -> deleteWorkflowBead -> ... -> List
```

That run was on a build of our fork. The ordering described below is the same on main, and the test below reproduces the defect there.

### Root cause

`run()` dispatches orders in a pre-readiness step, `startup-orders` (`cmd/gc/city_runtime.go:663-667`). It publishes readiness through `onStarted` only after that (`:781-783`). `markReady` at `:784` stops the startup watchdog.

`dispatchOrders` calls `runOrderTrackingRetentionWatchdog` synchronously (`:1509`). The watchdog's interval stamp starts at zero, so retention is due immediately (`:1674-1678`). When the backup and store checks allow it, the pass reads every closed tracking bead from each store it visits, all before readiness. It caps successful deletions at 100 across stores. Nothing bounds the time spent listing or running the delete guard checks.

`start_ready_timeout` does not bound this. It only sets how long `gc start` / `gc register` wait, and when the startup watchdog dumps goroutines.

The comment on `startup-orders` says the step exists so due orders don't wait behind maintenance work. Retention is maintenance work that runs inside that step.

### Reproduction

`TestCityRuntimeRun_ReadyBeforeRetentionSweep` is one test-only commit on main 7a34e556e: https://github.com/A3Ackerman/gascity/commit/12f49ddf683815d10cdd83ae1d9cbd3ab34dc49f

The test does three things:
1. It blocks the retention read.
2. It requires `OnStarted` to fire anyway.
3. It pokes the runtime and requires the retention read to happen within 10 seconds after `OnStarted`.

```sh
go test ./cmd/gc -run '^TestCityRuntimeRun_ReadyBeforeRetentionSweep$' -count=10
```

On 7a34e556e it fails 10 times out of 10:

```
order-tracking retention read reached before the city reported ready; the startup pass was NOT deferred
```

### Environment

- Test: main at 7a34e556e, macOS arm64.
- Incident: Linux amd64, supervisor-managed city, Dolt sql-server beads store, default `delete_after_close` (7d).

### Proposed fix

Skip only the retention watchdog during `startup-orders`, and leave its interval stamp unchanged so retention is still due on the first steady-state tick. This is the same boot-maintenance deferral #3811 used for #3288. With that change, the test passed 20 times out of 20 locally.

An alternative is to take retention off the tick entirely, on its own goroutine with single-flight. That is more than this bug needs.

I'm happy to open a PR with the test.

Related:
- #2604: order dispatch starving the tick in steady state.
- #3926: order-tracking retention growth.

snapshot.title: feat(sling): pre-flight gc sling --dry-run against a remote city
snapshot.body:
### What

`gc sling --dry-run` against a remote city context (`--context` / `--city-url` /
`GC_CITY_CONTEXT`) used to refuse outright:

```
gc sling: --dry-run is not supported for a remote city
```

so an operator holding a city context could not pre-flight a route. `--dry-run`
is now answered as a **read-only pre-flight**: it resolves the target, reads the
bead's class, evaluates the store agreement, prints what would happen, and
writes nothing. A real sling is unchanged.

### Why the refusal was the only wrong answer here

The check that actually costs you is the store agreement: **a cross-store route
silently wedges pools** (`tr-6s7yx`). With a blanket `--dry-run` refusal, the
only way to learn a route is cross-store is to attempt it. `--dry-run` exists
precisely to answer that question first, and a seat on a Mac pointed at a city
context is exactly where asking first matters most.

### Why the answer is computed from reads, not from a `dry_run` request field

This is the design question worth reviewing. The obvious implementation — put
`dry_run: true` on the existing `POST /v0/city/<c>/sling` body and let the
server run its own preview — is **unsafe against every already-deployed city**:
the hosted city decodes that body with `json.NewDecoder(...).Decode(v)` and no
`DisallowUnknownFields` (internal/api `decodeBody`), so a server running a gc
that predates the field silently *ignores* it and **performs the route**. There
is no version negotiation on that endpoint. A pre-flight that writes on the
version it has not talked to is worse than the refusal it replaces.

So `remoteSlingPreflight` answers from three reads the endpoint already answers
today, and never touches the mutating one:

| read | what it supplies |
|---|---|
| `GET /v0/city/<c>/config` | the hosted city's rigs (name/path/prefix) and agents (name/dir/scope) |
| `GET /v0/city/<c>/status` | the city root that projected agent dirs resolve against |
| `GET /v0/city/<c>/bead/<id>` | the bead's existence, class, status, current `gc.routed_to` |

It then calls the domain's **own** predicate — `agentutil.AgentReachesWorkflowStore`
— and returns the domain's **own** typed refusal, `sling.CrossStoreRouteError`.
The reachability rule is not restated in the CLI, so the pre-flight cannot drift
from the guard that enforces it. (Compare `gc storage preflight`, which is
described in the CHANGELOG by the same property: "every one of them the
migration's own function, not a copy".)

It reports what it could not determine instead of greenlighting it: an
unclassified bead prefix, or a target declaring a custom `work_query` (which the
local guard also skips), prints `not determined` rather than agreement.

### Scope discipline

* No new flag, env var, config key, wrapper, or second gate — this reuses the
  opt-in remote path that already ships (`resolveWriteTarget`, and the
  read-route precedent set by `gc events`).
* `--dry-run` is evaluated **after** every form refusal in `cmdSlingRemote`, so a
  `--dry-run` of a form a remote city cannot perform (`--stdin`, `--nudge`,
  `--on`, the 1-arg form, inline text) still refuses **before any request leaves
  the process**. Widening this flag widens nothing else.
* No local behaviour changes: nothing outside the remote branch was touched.

snapshot.title: bug: gc hook --claim work query can consume the whole claim window on a serialized shared dolt server while a direct bd claim completes in seconds
snapshot.body:
## Title

```
bug: hook --claim work query can consume the whole claim window on a serialized shared dolt server while a direct bd claim completes in seconds
```

## Summary

On a multi-rig city backed by a single shared (serialized) Dolt sql-server, `gc hook --claim --json`
repeatedly exceeds ~110 s and appears hung to the agent, while the same claim performed directly
(`bd ready` + `bd update <id> --claim`) completes in ~2 s and a bare `gc hook <agent> --json` returns
in ~15 s. The claim window is sized from the work-query timeout plus the mutation timeout
(`hookClaimWindowDefault = hookWorkQueryTimeout + hookClaimMutationTimeout`, `cmd_hook_claim.go`),
and the work query is bounded at 150 s (`cmd_hook.go`, raised 60→150 s on 2026-08-14 because the
~6-leg sequential probe was already exceeding 30 s under load). The design therefore *schedules*
multi-minute claim latencies on exactly the deployments (one Dolt server serving every rig's store)
the docs recommend, and the agent-visible behavior is indistinguishable from a hang.

## Environment

- macOS 27.0 (arm64), gc 1.4.1 via Homebrew (`beads` pinned 1.2.2, in-process NativeDoltStore active)
- One managed Dolt sql-server (127.0.0.1) serving **10 rig databases + hq** for a 10-rig city
- `probe_concurrency` unset → default 8 concurrent bd subprocess probes
  (`internal/config/config.go`: "bd serializes on a shared dolt sql-server, so unbounded
  parallelism causes contention" — the config comment itself names this contention mode)
- Contention source: pool scale-check + work-query probes from concurrent worker sessions and the
  reconciler, all hitting the same serialized server

## Reproduction

1. Run a multi-rig city (≥4 rigs, ~10 databases) on one shared Dolt server; have several workers
   and the reconciler issuing probes concurrently.
2. From a worker session run `gc hook <agent> --claim --json`.
3. Under load the command runs >110 s (observed repeatedly in production use, 2026-09-15); with the
   city idle the same command returns in ~11 s, and the non-claim hook returns in ~7-15 s.
4. Independently: `bd ready --json` (~1.4 s) and `bd update <id> --claim` (~2 s) complete against
   the same contended server.

Smallest observable differential (same server, same minute, idle city):

| Command | Wall time |
|---|---|
| `gc hook <agent> --json` (no claim) | ~7 s |
| `gc hook <agent> --claim --json` | ~11 s (loaded: >110 s) |
| `bd ready --json` | ~1.4 s |
| `bd update <id> --claim` | ~2 s |

## Expected behavior

An atomic claim should not be starved by the discovery probe. The claim CAS is a cheap single-store
mutation (`hookClaimMutationTimeout = 10 s`, correctly bounded); the expensive part is the
*federated routed-work query* in front of it, which re-runs the multi-leg probe (config comment:
"~6 sequential bd/store round-trips") on every claim attempt, serially competing with the very
contention it generates. Expected: claim latency stays O(mutation), discovery cost is capped or
cached, and a claim that finds work quickly claims it quickly.

## Actual behavior

- The work query legitimately runs up to 150 s (`hookWorkQueryTimeout`), and the claim window is
  derived from it (160 s total), so >110 s claim attempts are *by design* rather than a failure
  signal — but from the agent's seat they are indistinguishable from a hung process, and the
  documented work loop ("run `gc hook --claim`, repeat after closing") serializes this cost into
  every work item.
- Under concurrent probe load the serialized Dolt server makes each probe leg slower, so the
  system is at its worst exactly when the most workers are trying to claim: probe concurrency 8
  amplifies load; the raised 150 s bound converts the amplification into multi-minute waits.
- gascity's own history anticipates this shape: `cmd_hook.go` records 850+ `session.work_query_failed`
  events at the old 60 s bound ("every hook starved while `gc ready` run standalone returned the
  routed rows"). The bound was raised rather than the round-trip count reduced ("the real cure
  remains ga-4qdfn (fewer round-trips, faster reader)").

## Evidence

- Timing table above (production Mac, gc 1.4.1; >110 s observations from loaded city 2026-09-15)
- `cmd_hook.go:907-926` — `hookWorkQueryTimeout = 150s` with the 850+-events starvation history in
  the comment
- `cmd_hook_claim.go:58-85` — `hookClaimMutationTimeout = 10s`,
  `hookClaimWindowDefault = hookWorkQueryTimeout + hookClaimMutationTimeout`, comment: "a loaded
  multi-rig city's federated probe legitimately runs tens of seconds"
- `internal/config/config.go:2602-2607` — `probe_concurrency` default 8, comment naming bd
  serialization on a shared dolt sql-server as the contention cause
- `internal/doltpool/pool.go` — pooled *sql.DB handles with ReadTimeout/WriteTimeout 30 s exist for
  gc's Go-native paths; note `internal/api/convoy_sql.go:buildDoltDSN` sets dial `Timeout` but no
  `ReadTimeout`/`WriteTimeout`, so that path can hold a dead connection until TCP gives up
  (related, possibly distinct issue — flagging for triage)
- Transient CLOSE_WAIT connections on the client side observed during loaded windows (consistent
  with a response the client never reads back; not present at idle) — `lsof -nP -iTCP:<dolt-port>`

## Additional context

- Workers on this city now bypass `gc hook --claim` entirely (`bd ready` + `bd update --claim`)
  because the direct path is ~50× faster; this routes around atomic-claim bookkeeping, which is
  the integration smell that made us file.
- Possibly related known issue (same command, different failure mode): idle workers re-claim beads
  parked blocked-on-human, churning park/reclaim loops. Both suggest the claim protocol's
  discovery stage needs the rework ga-4qdfn anticipated.
- Suggested directions (maintainer's call): split claim into discover-fast (bounded, cheap,
  cache-friendly) + claim-fast (CAS, already bounded); let `--claim` accept a hint bead id;
  reduce probe round-trips per the existing ga-4qdfn note; expose claim-window progress so a
  multi-minute wait is distinguishable from a hang.

## Mitigation we ship locally (for the runbook PR, not upstream)

Documented in the cityworker work loop (`city/agents/cityworker/prompt.template.md`, "Work Loop →
KNOWN ISSUE 2026-09-15"): if `gc hook --claim` exceeds 60 s, fall back to
`gc bd ready --unassigned --sort oldest -t task --json` + `gc bd update <id> --claim`, verifying
assignee afterwards (command shape verified against gc 1.4.1: `--sort oldest` is the valid value,
not `created_at`). Race window acknowledged and accepted at city scale; explicit drain/no_work
results are still honored, timeouts are never treated as empty queues, and `gc hook --claim`
remains the primary path.

snapshot.title: docs(deps): record why the bd pin cannot move to a newer-numbered release
snapshot.body:
## Summary

`deps.env` has long carried an instruction to promote `BD_VERSION` off `v1.1.0` "the day" beads publishes a release with the `--if-assignee`/`--if-status` conditional-write flags. beads has since shipped `v1.2.1` and `v1.2.2`, both dated after those flags landed in [beads#5008](https://github.com/gastownhall/beads/pull/5008), so the pin looked promotable. It isn't. The reason is one the old comment couldn't have anticipated: a beads tag's number doesn't order its capabilities.

beads cuts stable hotfixes off the `v1.1.0` line, which branched three weeks before the flags landed. That line is linear, it never merged to main, and both `v1.1.2` and the newest **stable** release `v1.2.2` sit on it. Neither one carries `--if-assignee` at all. `v1.2.1` is the first release that clears beads#5008 and it does carry both flags, but GitHub marks it a prerelease, so it doesn't meet the published bar this pin holds the installable default to.

So the pin stays where it is, and this change records why. It rewrites the `BD_VERSION` rationale in `deps.env`, names the two conditions that gate the next attempt, and sweeps the now-falsified "no published release has the flags" claim out of the five other places that asserted it: the `BD_PREV_VERSION` floor note, three comments across `internal/beads`, and the integration test's skip-and-fatal message. That last one is the one to look at, since it's the only site a human reads at runtime. **Comments and messages only: every pinned value is byte-identical to main.**

```mermaid
gitGraph
   commit id: "v1.1.0 base"
   branch hotfix-line
   commit id: "v1.1.2 (no flags)"
   commit id: "v1.2.2 (no flags, STABLE)"
   checkout main
   commit id: "beads#5008 flags"
   commit id: "v1.2.1 (flags, PRERELEASE)"
   commit id: "main"
```

## Risk

There's none to CI behaviour. No pinned version, SHA, or workflow `BD_VERSION` block moves, so every job installs exactly the bd it installed before. If CI goes red here, it won't be from this diff.

<details> <summary>Verification, and the two conditions that gate promotion</summary>

### How each claim was checked

Capability was measured against the published tarballs rather than inferred from version numbers, which is the same method the original comment used for `v1.1.2`:

| Release | Published | GitHub state | `bd update --help` names `--if-assignee` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `v1.1.2` | 2026-07-26 | stable | no |
| `v1.2.1` | 2026-08-11 | prerelease | **yes**, with the exit-13 semantics |
| `v1.2.2` | 2026-08-15 | stable | no |

Ancestry, via the compare API against `gastownhall/beads`:

- The hotfix line is linear and rooted before the flags: [`8e4e59d39`](https://github.com/gastownhall/beads/commit/8e4e59d39f3459a43cf21a3236a13eca4dd874f7) (2026-07-04) → +4 → `v1.1.2` → +7 → `v1.2.2`.
- Neither `v1.1.2` nor `v1.2.2` is an ancestor of beads `main`; each holds commits main does not.
- `v1.2.1` **is** an ancestor of beads `main` (main is 9 commits ahead, `v1.2.1` behind by none), and [`6e8af8bf8`](https://github.com/gastownhall/beads/commit/6e8af8bf8) is an ancestor of `v1.2.1`.

### Two conditions gate the next attempt

1. beads publishes a non-prerelease release cut from main, and its per-platform tarball SHAs go into `.github/scripts/install-bd-archive.sh`.
2. The fresh managed-Dolt bootstrap fix in [#5294](https://github.com/gastownhall/gascity/pull/5294) lands first. bd 1.2 added a legacy-workspace guard that refuses a pre-existing `.beads/dolt` carrying no version witness, so a fresh city under a 1.2 pin fails init until the witness is written for a proven-fresh database. That PR is open as of this writing.

Until both hold, the only flag-capable bd CI can obtain stays the source-built `BD_CURRENT_REF` cell, which is where the `ReleaseIfCurrent` CAS contract already runs.

### Every site the claim appeared in

| File | Site | Action |
|---|---|---|
| `deps.env` | `BD_VERSION` rationale | rewritten |
| `deps.env` | `BD_PREV_VERSION` floor note | corrected |
| `internal/beads/bdstore_conditional_release.go` | package comment | corrected |
| `internal/beads/bdstore.go` | `ReleaseIfCurrent` doc comment | corrected |
| `internal/beads/bdstore_conditional_release_integration_test.go` | test doc comment | corrected |
| `internal/beads/bdstore_conditional_release_integration_test.go` | skip and fatal message | corrected, runtime-visible |

Three further sites were checked and deliberately left alone, each re-verified as still true: the `.github/workflows/ci.yml` comment saying `BD_VERSION` "is a published release that predates it"; `bdstore_test.go`; and the graduation test, which is about `--if-revision`, a different flag absent from both `v1.2.1` and `v1.2.2`.

### Checks run

- `sh -n deps.env`, and sourcing it to confirm `BD_VERSION` and `BD_PREV_VERSION` read back unchanged.
- `diff` of the non-comment lines against `origin/main`: identical.
- `gofmt -l`, `go build ./internal/beads/...`, `go vet ./internal/beads/...`: all clean, before and after the round-1 sweep.
- Test packages under `internal/beads` compile; nothing asserts on any string touched.
- `git diff --check`: clean.

</details>

snapshot.title: No cap for one template family across rigs: max_active_sessions can bound a workspace, a rig, or one template in one rig — never one template everywhere
snapshot.body:
## Summary

`max_active_sessions` can bound a **workspace**, a **rig**, or **one template in
one rig** — but there is no way to bound **one template summed across every
rig**. On a multi-rig city that is the cap an operator actually needs for any
resource the rigs share, and the host is the obvious one.

## The scopes that exist

Revision `dfb4d5ab5` (2026-07-30), `internal/config/`:

| Struct | File:line | Scope |
|---|---|---|
| `Workspace` | `config.go:1304` | whole city, **all** templates |
| `Rig` | `config.go:623` | one rig, **all** templates |
| `Agent` | `config.go:3176` | one rig, one template |
| `AgentOverride` | `config.go:785` | one rig, one template |
| `AgentPatch` | `patch.go:148` | one rig, one template |

Every scope is either "all templates in a scope" or "one template in one rig".
The cell that is missing is "one template, every rig".

## Why it matters

Our city has 13 rigs. Each has a `gc.implementation-worker` pool, and those are
the sessions that run builds and test suites — `go test -p=4`, `cargo`,
`vitest`. They are the ones that cost the host.

What we want to say is one sentence:

> at most 6 `gc.implementation-worker` sessions may run at once, across all rigs

There is no way to say it.

- `Workspace.MaxActiveSessions` (32 here) bounds *every* session, so it also
  counts the always-on roster, dispatchers, planners, reviewers and publishers —
  ~26 sessions that cost almost nothing. Setting it to 6 would starve the city.
- Per-rig or per-agent caps only bound one rig. Thirteen caps of 1 is not a cap
  of 6: it is a cap of 13 that also stops a single rig from ever using spare
  capacity when the others are idle.

Measured here on 2026-09-14: 13 rigs, every `implementation-worker` with
`ScaleCheck ""` and `MaxActiveSessions null`, all bounded only by the workspace
cap of 32 — on a 24-core host. That is how we got to load 29.

## What we did instead

A federation-owned `scale_check` on every worker pool, sharing one `flock`ed
ledger under the city's `.gc/`, that computes a city-wide allocation from one
snapshot and prints each rig's share. It works, and it is ~1,000 lines of bash
that exists only because the engine cannot express the sentence above. It is
also not strict — see the companion filing on the cold-wake merge, which is the
one overshoot we cannot remove from outside.

## What would fix it

A template-family cap resolved across rigs. Shape we would use, but any spelling
works:

```toml
[[template_caps]]
template = "gc.implementation-worker"   # local name, matched across every rig
max_active_sessions = 6
```

Enforced where the per-rig nested caps are already applied (`applyNestedCaps`),
so admission order and the existing "in-flight and resuming first" behaviour
carry over unchanged. That would let us delete the ledger, the allocator and
most of the arithmetic and keep only the reporting.

## Notes

- Not urgent for us — we have the workaround shipping. Filing it because the
  workaround is the kind of thing that should not need to exist, and because the
  next city with a shared host will hit the same wall.
- Happy to prototype it if the shape is agreeable.

snapshot.title: fix(beads): carry bd's blocked status through the read model
snapshot.body:
## Problem

`mapBdStatus` collapses bd's six statuses to three, and the collapse erases `blocked`. Four read paths share the function (`BdStore` decode, `DoltliteReadStore`, `NativeDoltStore`, and `EncodeBeadEventPayload`), so no response can carry the state. One bead, three sources at one moment:

```
curl -s 'http://127.0.0.1:8372/v0/city/<name>/beads?limit=1000'
  -> {"id":"sc-lm3zj","status":"open"}
bd show sc-lm3zj --json   -> "status":"blocked"
bd list --limit 0 --json  -> "status":"blocked"
```

The whole-list histogram from that endpoint read 497 open, 3 in_progress, and 0 blocked, while bd reported 48 blocked in the same city. `in_progress` survives, so the projection is not collapsing everything; it loses `blocked` specifically. The dashboard then reported 99 beads as needing a human when 26 of them were finished work blocked only on a handoff claim.

The DTO's `is_blocked` column does not recover the state: it answers bd's different, dependency-derived question and reads 0 for explicitly blocked beads.

## Change

Widen the status set rather than compensate in the frontend. `mapBdStatus` returns `"blocked"`, so every reader sees it. `review` and `testing` still collapse to `open`, because no consumer distinguishes them.

`blocked` joins the open **set** instead of becoming a third terminal state, which keeps the change reporting-only:

- `beads.IsOpenStatus` reports membership in that set. The 38 demand, claim, dispatch, route-recovery, sling, and mail guards that mean "still open" ask it instead of comparing to `"open"`.
- `ListQuery.Matches` treats `Status:"open"` as the set. That is already what the native store's `ExcludeStatus{closed, in_progress}` filter returns, and `native_dolt_store_count.go` documents the mismatch. Exact equality there would have silently dropped every blocked bead from each `Status:"open"` list, changing demand, claim, and mail behavior.
- Ready stays narrower on purpose: `IsReadyCandidateForTier` still compares the status exactly, mirroring `nativeDoltOpenReadyStatuses`, because bd's own ready semantics exclude blocked (ga-3mv5d3).

The dashboard Beads page and the attention badge are untouched; both are correct on correct data.

## Consumer audit

51 non-test sites compared a status to `"open"`. 38 are guards on a decoded bead that must keep treating blocked as open, and they now call `IsOpenStatus`. The rest stay exact, each for a reason:

| Site | Why it stays exact |
| --- | --- |
| `beads.IsReadyCandidateForTier` | Mirrors `nativeDoltOpenReadyStatuses`; bd excludes blocked from ready. |
| `MemStore.Reopen`, `SQLiteStore.Reopen` | A blocked bead must still reopen to `open`. |
| `EncodeBeadEventPayload` | Restores an indefinite deferral, which only bd's `deferred` sets. |
| `session.sessionMatchesFilters` | Pinned twin-equivalence contract with `sessionMatchesFiltersInfo`; a non-closed session bead still matches through the `state` filter. |
| `native_dolt_store.go`, `native_dolt_store_count.go`, `caching_store_writes.go` | Query and write inputs, not decoded statuses. |

## Tests

- `internal/beads/blocked_status_test.go` pins blocked through the mapping, `normalizedBdReadState`, the open set, a `Status:"open"` list, an exact `Status:"blocked"` list, and the Ready exclusion.
- Repinned the two tables that asserted the old collapse: `TestBdStoreStatusMapping` and `TestNativeDoltStoreMapsUpstreamStatusesToGasCityContract`.
- `TestNativeDoltStoreListStatusOpenMatchesOpenNormalizedUpstreamStatuses` keeps its membership assertion; its per-row check now asserts open-set membership.
- `MemStore` was the one store that dropped a literal blocked row from an open list, so `TestCachingStorePartialPrimeRefusesUnknownDependencyStatus` changed premise. It now pins the refusal with a closed dependency, which genuinely is outside the primed snapshot, and a new `TestCachingStorePartialPrimeKnowsBlockedDependency` pins that a blocked dependency is inside it and still blocks its dependent.
- Refreshed the comments that described the old collapse, in product code and in the tests that model the hazard.

## Verification

```
gofmt -l ./cmd ./internal              # clean
go vet ./internal/beads ./cmd/gc ./internal/api
go test ./internal/beads/...           # ok
go test ./internal/api/...             # ok
go test ./internal/mail/... ./internal/dispatch/... ./internal/sling/... \
        ./internal/nudgequeue/... ./internal/session/... ./internal/orders/...   # ok
go test ./cmd/gc/                      # see below
```

`cmd/gc` reports 121 failures on this machine, and all of them are environmental: 118 fail because a local PATH guard refuses `git -c core.hooksPath` inside the worktree-reaper fixtures, two init tests fail on the same guard during `git clone`, and `TestStopManagedCityBoundsForcedShutdownWhenRuntimeHangs` misses a 120 ms timing budget. The three non-guard failures reproduce identically in an untouched checkout at base. The status-sensitive subset passes:

```
go test ./cmd/gc/ -run 'Blocked|Demand|RouteRecovery|DetachedOrphan|PoolIdle|NamedTrigger|Treadmill|AwakeBridge|SessionName'   # ok
```

`internal/runtime/herdr` does not compile at `ca8c28edc` (`panebinding_provider_test.go` return-value mismatches), which is unrelated to this change.

## Summary

Fixes #5552. Supersedes the stale #5560 (same design, rebased onto current `main`, which had already moved the OpenCode hook to v6 for #5563) and extends it to the MiMo Code plugin, which has the identical shape.

OpenCode fires `experimental.chat.system.transform` from `Agent.generate`, once per model generation, and `chat.message` once more per user message. Both call `buildPrefix()`, so every tool call in a turn ran `gc nudge drain --inject` and `gc mail check --inject` again. Two consequences:

- The drain is consumptive, so the queue was emptied several times per turn and the drained items landed in whichever generation won the race.

snapshot.body:
The "Current integration mission" section in `AGENTS.md` is written from the perspective of one specific downstream fork — its mission, its local directory paths, and its remote naming — and none of that carries over to anyone else's fork or to this repo.

That raises a question that changes what actually needs fixing: is the intent that nobody works directly in `gastownhall/gascity`, and that all real work happens in forks that get integrated here? I'm assuming so, and if that's right I'm honestly fine with `AGENTS.md` being written from a downstream fork's point of view. But three things still don't hold up even under that assumption.

**It assumes I named the remote `upstream`.** The feature archaeology block runs `git fetch upstream`, `git diff upstream/main...HEAD`, `git range-diff upstream/main...HEAD`. That only works if I added `gastownhall/gascity` as a remote and happened to call it `upstream`. A fresh fork clone just has `origin`, and nothing in the doc says to add it. Either say so up front, or don't depend on the name.

**It has paths from someone's machine.** `/data/projects/gascity` and `/data/projects/t3code` aren't going to exist for anyone else.

**It states what the fork is for.** "This fork is integrating Gas City + T3 Code + a DoltLite-backed beads store." If everyone's working in a fork, every fork exists for its own reason — mine has nothing to do with T3 Code. Same with "Do not bury T3 Code or DoltLite assumptions in generic SDK paths," and "This fork has repeatedly lost working code during branch churn," which is one fork's history, not mine.

The rest of the section is good and I'd keep it: the archaeology workflow, "treat archived plans and audits as evidence, not gospel," and keeping backend-specific behavior behind the runtime/config/beads boundaries. That all applies to any fork. It just shouldn't be tied to one fork's mission.

For context, the section came in whole with a963419a1 (#2474), so I suspect it was never re-scoped rather than being deliberate.

If the fork-only assumption is right, this looks like a small edit — drop the specific mission and the local paths, and name the remote the git commands expect. Happy to send a PR. If it's not right, the section probably needs a bigger rethink, since read from inside this repo it's just false.

I searched for existing issues on this (`AGENTS.md`, "this fork", "integration mission", "T3 Code") and didn't find anything.

snapshot.title: orders: an order that stops firing is silent — no liveness/overdue detection
snapshot.body:
## Summary

A scheduled order that stops firing is indistinguishable from one that is merely
not due, and nothing detects the difference. In our city `pr-watch` went **six
days without executing** and the only symptom was silence — the thing it was
watching (approved PRs) piled up, and an APPROVED-and-CONFLICTING PR sat
unattended until a human happened to look.

The proximate cause was a cron parse gap now fixed by 63a3b9fc7 (#5711) —
`cronFieldMatches` had no range support, so `0 7-19 * * 1-5` could never match.
Verified by running the pre-fix function in isolation:

```
field="7-19"  value=12 -> false      field="12"             value=12 -> true
field="7-19"  value=19 -> false      field="*"              value=12 -> true
field="1-5"   value=3  -> false      field="7,8,9,10,11,12" value=12 -> true
```

**This issue is not about that parse bug.** #5711 fixes the specific cause and
adds load-time validation, which is the right first line of defense. The residual
problem is the general one: *when an order stops running for any reason, nothing
notices.* Load-time validation catches unparseable schedules; it cannot catch an
order that parses fine and stops firing anyway (exec repeatedly failing, a
dispatch path starved as in #3368, a trigger evaluated but never dispatched).

## Why this failure mode is especially bad

An order is usually a watchdog. When a watchdog dies quietly, the operator stops
checking manually *because* the watchdog exists — so the outage lasts far longer
than if there had been no automation at all. Silence has to mean "nothing is
stuck", never "nothing is happening".

## Suggested shape

Some form of overdue detection: for any order with a schedule, compare `last_run`
against the schedule's expected previous occurrence and surface anything overdue
by more than a small multiple of its nominal interval. `gc doctor` already knows
how to parse schedules after #5711, so the schedule→expected-occurrence half
exists.

Two design notes from our post-mortem, offered rather than prescribed:

1. **The last line of defense should have no configuration surface.** A watchdog
   watching a watchdog is circular; the recursion has to bottom out in something
   too simple to misconfigure — ideally one hardcoded rule with no schedule of its
   own, so its only failure mode is the supervisor itself dying, which is loud.
2. **Overrun is a related but separate case.** An order whose exec outlives its
   own interval can overlap itself (cooldown measures from run *start*). Naive
   locking turns "sometimes overruns" into "never runs again", which is the same
   silent-failure class — so any locking wants to be stale-tolerant and to log
   loudly when it steals a lock.

## Environment

`gc` built from `26e136d13` (2026-08-19). The parse gap is fixed upstream at
`63a3b9fc7`; the liveness gap appears to remain — `git ls-tree` on `origin/main`
shows `bead_worktree_liveness*` but nothing for order liveness, and no
heartbeat/overdue handling in `internal/orders/cron.go`.

snapshot.title: feat(controller): deliver queued nudges on provider idle events
snapshot.body:
The controller now delivers a queued nudge as soon as the provider reports that
session idle, instead of leaving it to be picked up by the next patrol pass.

For an event-capable provider such as herdr, the provider already pushes session
events and the runtime already receives them. Until now the only consumer was
the provider's own activity reporting, so a queued nudge waited for the periodic
sweep. That sweep interval is the floor on delivery latency, and only while the
controller keeps up: passes run one at a time, so a busy controller stretches it
further.

## What changed

`cmd/gc/nudge_event_dispatcher.go` is new. It subscribes to provider session
events and runs a delivery pass when a session goes idle. The pass is bounded
and cancellable:

- Concurrent pass starts are capped at eight. A pass that cannot get a slot
  waits rather than being dropped.
- A kick that arrives while a pass already holds the same key is recorded with
  its retry budget and re-armed when that pass finishes, so a sweep is deferred
  rather than lost.
- Shutdown abandons a pass that has not started. Cancellation is checked on its
  own before the code races for a slot, because a single `select` over both
  gives neither case priority and would let the pass run anyway roughly half the
  time.
- Each session's delivery runs on its own goroutine, so one slow pane does not
  serialize the rest.

`cmd/gc/cmd_nudge.go` stops spawning a per-session poller sidecar when an
event-capable provider is in use and a controller is actually answering for the
city. It fails open: with no controller, nothing hosts the replacement, so the
poller still spawns and the queue still drains. Liveness is answered by asking
the running system, not by reading a status file.

`cmd/gc/city_runtime.go` starts and stops the dispatcher with the controller and
re-points it across a provider-changing reload.

Related to #6361, which reports that poller suppression decides from config
alone without checking that the dispatcher is running. This does not close it.
The liveness helper added here (`nudgePollerDispatcherIsLive`) guards only the
event-capable-provider path; the supervisor-mode branch above it still returns
on config alone, which is the case #6361 describes. A fix for that issue can
reuse this helper.

## Test plan

- `go build ./...` and `go vet ./...`: pass.
- `go test ./cmd/gc/...`: pass, 274s.
- `go test ./cmd/gc/ -run 'TestNudgeEventDispatcher.*' -race -count=3`: pass,
  all 22 dispatcher tests green on every run.
- The shutdown case is asserted over 200 calls per run rather than one. A single
  call cannot distinguish the two behaviours, because the race it replaces came
  out the right way about half the time. Measured before the fix: the pass ran
  in 103 of 200 trials. After: none, across 1000 trials.
- Reviewed by a panel that included a second model from a different provider,
  since every commit here was written by the same one.

## Known limitations

Each of these is known, accepted, and tracked in #6367.

1. `runtime.Provider.Nudge` takes no context and the herdr client applies no
   default timeout, so nothing bounds one delivery's own lifetime. A pane that
   wedges permanently parks its goroutine for the life of the process. The slot
   cap bounds concurrent starts, not goroutine lifetime.
2. Following from that, an abandoned delivery can write its post-delivery stamp
   after shutdown has closed the store.
3. A provider-changing reload is not fenced against a delivery already in
   flight, so a nudge can be acknowledged for a session that is being stopped on
   the old provider at the same moment.
4. The `gc prime` hook path constructs a session provider on every invocation,
   which is a hook-frequency path where latency matters.
5. The shutdown check narrows the race rather than closing it. Cancellation
   landing between the check and the slot acquisition can still let one call
   through. That is materially smaller than what it replaces, which affected
   roughly half of all calls for the whole shutdown window, but it is real.

snapshot.title: fix(api): resolve a pool session's recorded runtime name in gc status (ga-7n2hhq)
snapshot.body:
Fixes the false-outage class behind ga-7n2hhq: `gc status --json` reports
`running:false` for an agent whose seat is alive and working. On 2026-09-16
this reached the mayor as a false P0 against a `gascity/deployer` that was
working normally and had just passed the full suite.

## Root cause

`gc status` derived every agent's session name canonically
(`internal/api/handler_status.go:251` → `agent.SessionNameFor`). But a pool
instance's runtime name is minted by a **separate** derivation:
`poolRuntimeSessionName` (`cmd/gc/session_name_lookup.go:489`) steps aside
onto a `-pool` suffixed name when a configured named session reserves the
bare one, or for a transient slot.

That step-aside is *sanctioned* — it exists so a pool can coexist with a
configured named session on the same agent — and it is recorded on the
session bead. It cannot be re-derived from the agent identity. So status
probed `gascity--deployer` while the seat actually ran as
`gascity--deployer-pool`, `IsRunning` returned false, and a live seat was
reported dead.

Two independent derivations of one naming contract; only the create side
knew the whole rule.

## The session-snapshot timeout is NOT the cause

The incident report blamed the `partial:true` session-snapshot timeout. That
is coincident, not causal, and it is worth being explicit because the
obvious "fix" would not have prevented this:

1. **By source:** the `running` field comes from `statusProviderRunning` →
   `sp.IsRunning` (`handler_status.go:1091-1097`). It never reads the
   snapshot, so a snapshot timeout cannot change it.
2. **By experiment:** the tests here run with a **healthy** snapshot — they
   assert no `sessions:` partial error is present — and still reproduce
   `running:false`. The positive control (same capacity shape, same healthy
   snapshot, canonical session name) passes. The session *name* is the only
   variable that changes the verdict.

So reporting `running: null` under `partial:true` would not have prevented
this incident. It may have merit on its own, but it is a separate concern
and is deliberately not in this PR.

## Fix

New helper `statusRuntimeSessionName` resolves the runtime name from the
session snapshot the status path **already holds** — no new I/O. Strongest
evidence first:

1. a session bead sitting on the canonical name — today's behavior, kept
   exactly, so canonically named sessions are unaffected;
2. a bead whose recorded `agent_name` IS this instance — the shape
   production writes (`cmd/gc/build_desired_state.go:4836` sets
   `identityAgentName` to the qualified instance, falling back to the
   template);
3. for a single-instance identity, the one bead recorded against it.

Anything ambiguous falls back to the canonical name rather than guessing.

The data was already in hand: `statusSessionSnapshot` carries a `byTemplate`
index and `appendUnlimitedPoolSessionBeads` already used it — but returned
early for **any** bounded-capacity agent (`*maxSess >= 0`), which is exactly
the `min=0`/`max=1` shape that an explicit `MinActiveSessions` creates
(`internal/config/session_capacity.go:123`).

### Note for reviewers

`statusSessionQualifiedName` looks like the right matching helper and is
**not**: it maps `gascity--deployer-pool` to `gascity/deployer-pool`, not to
the agent identity `gascity/deployer`, so matching on it silently fails.
That is the trap a re-derivation of this fix would most likely fall into.

## Tests

`internal/api/handler_status_pool_identity_test.go` — 5 tests, each verified
**RED at a41b91a032** and **GREEN** with the change:

- `TestStatusReportsPoolSuffixedSessionAsRunning` — the incident
- `TestStatusReportsPoolSuffixedSessionAsRunningWithRecordedAgentName` — the
  bead shape production actually persists
- `TestStatusMapsEachPoolInstanceToItsOwnSession` — multi-instance; fails if
  instances are cross-wired onto each other's sessions
- `TestStatusReportsCanonicallyNamedSessionAsRunning` — positive control
- `TestStatusKeepsUnlimitedPoolAgentVisible` — positive control

Gates: full `internal/api` package passes (exit 0), `go vet` clean,
`go build ./...` clean, pre-commit hooks active and passed (`lint-changed`
0 issues), pre-push suite reported all fast jobs passed.

## Relationship to ga-rkbqnc.2.4 (open, ready-to-build)

Complementary, **not** duplicate. `ga-rkbqnc.2.4` normalizes
`SupportsInstanceExpansion` (create-side, `session_capacity.go`); its own
audit in `ga-rkbqnc.2.1` records that all five `internal/api` packages stay
green under that change. It does not touch this read-side resolution, and it
would not have fixed this — a live session keeps the name it was created
with. Different files, no collision.

## Scope / impact

No wire or API change (`StatusAgentDetail` is unchanged), no new
abstraction. Consumers using `gc status` as a liveness probe stop seeing
working pool seats as dead. Behavior for canonically named sessions is
unchanged by construction (resolution step 1).

snapshot.title: feat(beads): model bd's created_by, owner, notes and gate condition on Bead
snapshot.body:
First of the three parts split out of #4912, at @quad341's request. It stands alone and does not depend on the others.

## What it does

bd emits `created_by`, `owner`, `notes`, `await_type` and `await_id` on its JSON projections. `Bead` modelled none of them, so every store dropped them on decode and a bead read through `gc` showed strictly less than the same bead read through `bd`. A gate bead reported no condition at all — the thing it is waiting on was simply not carried.

All five are **read-only projections**. No write path persists any of them: they are absent from `Create`'s argument list, from `UpdateOpts`, and from every exec create/update request shape. Setting one on a `Bead` handed to `Create` is silently dropped. Populate them through bd (`bd gate create`, `bd update --notes`, …) and read them back here.

## Why per store

Each backend decodes its own row shape, so a column dropped in one is invisible to the others. Covered in all four: bd exec, native Dolt, DoltLite, and the caching layer.

## Given / When / Then

- **Given** a bead created with `bd update --notes`, **when** it is read through any store, **then** `Notes` carries the text instead of an empty string.
- **Given** a gate bead with `await_type=gh:pr` and an await id, **when** it is read, **then** both are carried, so a consumer can say what the gate waits on.
- **Given** a bead on a store whose schema predates these columns, **when** it is read, **then** the fields are empty and nothing else changes.
- **Given** a `Bead` with `CreatedBy` set handed to `Create`, **when** it is written, **then** the value is dropped — these are projections, not writable fields.

## Size

The hand-written change is ~35 KB. `Bead` is projected into the generated OpenAPI spec, so the five json tags necessarily regenerate the spec, genclient, TS types and the SPA bundle; those are mechanical, and the bundle assets differ only in content hashes (`23 files changed, 0 insertions, 0 deletions`). Whole patch is ~47 KB, against ~1.0 MB for the combined change.

## Scope

`internal/beads/{beads,bdstore,native_dolt_store,doltlite_read_store,caching_store_events}.go`, `internal/beads/exec/{exec,json}.go`, per-store column tests, plus the regenerated spec/client/bundle.

## Related work

- #4912 — the combined change this is split from; parts 2 (`gc bd` bridge) and 3 (API projection) follow once this lands.
